newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FOCUS - Kuwait parliament amends, approves budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kuwait parliament amends, approves budget.

text.p: Kuwait's parliament on Tuesday approved a 4.378 billion dinar ($14.38 billion) state budget for 1997/98 after increasing the net deficit to 1.274 billion dinars by rejecting plans to increase income from higher charges.
Total revenues were cut to 3.105 billion dinars after parliament rejected a government assumption of earning some 203 million dinars more from raising rates for some public services.
MPs argued that the government could only raise charges after parliamentary approval. The government agreed to cut non-oil revenue by 95 million dinars to 550 million dinars.

The new budget, following legal provisions, will continue to inject fresh funds into Kuwait's foreign investment "egg" by depositing 10 percent of total revenues in the portfolio, raising the gross deficit to 1.584 billion dinars.
The value of Kuwait's global holdings is a state secret but banking sources estimate the current worth of the investment portifolio at around $40 billion.

"Preliminary estimates indicate that our return on investment in 1996/97 (July-June) could exceed the state's 1995/96 oil revenue of more than three billion dinars," Ali al- Bader, head of the state investment arm, the Kuwait Investment Authority, told Reuters.
But economists say that that KIA should not calculate the appreciation in the value of its holdings as a return on investment.

The 4.21 billion dinar 1996/97 budget carried a projected net deficit of 1.21 billion dinars and a gross deficit of 1.51 billion, which was cut considerably due to a rise in oil prices in 1996 by some $5 a barrel above budget projections.
Revenue from Kuwait's two million barrels per day OPEC oil quota would be almost unchanged in the new budget at 2.555 billion dinars, according to a conservative estimate of $13 a barrel.
But industry experts expect oil earnings to exceed forecasts again.
The Defence Ministry was allocated around 495 million dinars, which political sources said did not include the cost of rebuilding the military after the 1990 Iraqi invasion.

Kuwait launched a $12 billion plan after the 1991 Gulf War to rebuild the army and has concluded several deals since then, mainly with the United States, Britain, France and Russia. Other contracts are in the pipeline.
Out of a total allocation of some 312 million dinars, the Interior Ministry is expected to spend about 278 million dinars on salaries, while Defence Ministry salaries were put at 10.6 million dinars.
Total state salaries are forecast to eat away more than half of the country's projected oil earnings for 1997/98.
The welfare state offers the 710,000 Kuwaiti citizens generous salaries and benefits unmatched by the private sector. It employs around 92 percent of the Kuwaiti workforce.
The head of state, Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, was allocated eight million dinars in the new budget, while court expenses were put at 24 million dinars.
